l: Harrison Ford
Harrison Ford (born July 13, 1942) is an American actor. Regarded as a cinematic cultural icon, Ford's accolades
include nominations for an <color=#3366CC>Academy Award</color>, a <color=#3366CC>British Academy Film Award</color>, two <color=#3366CC>Emmy Awards</color>, five <color=#3366CC>Golden Globes</color>
and two SAG-AFTRA's Actor Awards. He is also the recipient of the AFI Life Achievement Award, Cecil B. DeMille
Award, Honorary César, Honorary Palme d'Or and SAG-AFTRA Life Achievement Award.
After making his screen debut in 1966 and early supporting roles in the films American Graffiti (1973) and The
Conversation (1974), Ford achieved global stardom for portraying Han Solo in the <color=#3366CC>space opera</color> film <color=#3366CC>Star Wars</color> (1977), a
role he reprised in four subsequent films for the eponymous franchise spanning the next four decades. He also
received recognition for his portrayal of <color=#3366CC>the titular character</color> in the Indiana Jones franchise (1981–2023); Rick Deckard
in the Blade Runner franchise (1982–2017); and Jack Ryan in the action thriller films Patriot Games (1992) and Clear
and Present Danger (1994). These roles established him as an action hero and one of <color=#3366CC>Hollywood</color>'s most bankable
stars from the late 1970s into the early 2000s.
Ford's performance in the thriller film Witness (1985) earned him his sole <color=#3366CC>Oscar</color> nomination for Best Actor. His other
films include The Mosquito Coast (1986); Working Girl (1988); Presumed Innocent (1990); The Fugitive (1993); Sabrina
(1995); The Devil's Own (1997); Air Force One (1997); Six Days, Seven Nights (1998); What Lies Beneath (2000);
K-19: The Widowmaker (2002); Cowboys & Aliens (2011); 42 (2013); The Age of Adaline (2015); The Call of the Wild
(2020); and Captain America: Brave New World (2025). Ford has also starred in the Paramount+ western series 1923
(2022–2025) and the Apple TV+ comedy series Shrinking (since 2023), earning two nominations at the <color=#3366CC>Primetime</color>
<color=#3366CC>Emmy Awards</color> for the latter.
Outside acting, Ford is a licensed pilot. He has often assisted the emergency services in rescue missions near his
home in <color=#3366CC>Wyoming</color> and he chaired an aviation education program for youth from 2004 to 2009. Ford is also an
environmental activist, having served as the inaugural vice chair of Conservation International since 1991.
Early life and education
Harrison Ford was born on July 13, 1942, at the Swedish Covenant Hospital in the Lincoln Square community area of
Chicago, Illinois, to Dorothy (née Nidelman) and advertising executive and former vaudeville and radio actor John
William "Christopher" Ford. His mother has been described as a radio actress, but Harrison Ford denies this, and the
attribution may be due to confusion with the unrelated actress and model Dorothy Ford.
Ford's younger brother, Terence, was born in 1945. Their father was an Irish Catholic, while their mother was an
Ashkenazi Jew whose parents were emigrants from <color=#3366CC>Minsk</color>, Belarus, then in the Russian Empire. When asked in which
religion he and his brother were raised, Ford jokingly responded "<color=#3366CC>Democrat</color>" and more seriously stated that they were
raised to be "liberals of every stripe". When asked about what influence his Jewish and Irish Catholic ancestry may
have had on him, he quipped, "As a man I've always felt Irish, as an actor I've always felt Jewish."
Ford was a Boy Scout, achieving the second-highest rank of Life Scout. He worked at Napowan Adventure Base Scout
Camp as a counselor for the Reptile Study merit badge. Because of this, he and director <color=#3366CC>Steven Spielberg</color> later
decided to depict the young <color=#3366CC>Indiana Jones</color> as a Life Scout in Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade (1989). Ford
graduated in 1960 from Maine East High School in Park Ridge, Illinois. His voice was the first student voice broadcast
on his high school's new radio station, WMTH, and he was its first sportscaster during his senior year. He attended
Ripon College in Ripon, Wisconsin, where he was a philosophy major and a member of the Sigma Nu fraternity. A
self-described "late bloomer", Ford took a drama class in the final quarter of his senior year to get over his shyness and
became fascinated with acting. Ford was expelled from college for plagiarism four days before graduation.
Career
1964–1976: Early work
In 1964, after a season of summer stock with the Belfry Players in Wisconsin, Ford traveled to Los Angeles and
eventually signed a contract with <color=#3366CC>Columbia Pictures</color>' new talent program. His first known role was an uncredited one as
a bellhop in Dead Heat on a Merry-Go-Round (1966). There is little record of his non-speaking (or "extra") roles in film.
Ford was at the bottom of the hiring list, having offended producer Jerry Tokofsky. According to one anecdote,
Tokofsky told Ford that when actor <color=#3366CC>Tony Curtis</color> delivered a bag of groceries, he could tell that Curtis was a movie star
whereas Ford was not; Ford immediately retorted that if Curtis was truly a talented actor, he would have delivered them
like a bellhop. Ford was apparently fired soon after. In 1970 Ford met Patricia McQueeney, who would go on to work as
his agent and manager.
His speaking roles continued next with Luv (1967), though he was still uncredited. He was finally credited as "Harrison
J. Ford" in the 1967 <color=#3366CC>Western</color> film A Time for Killing, starring <color=#3366CC>Glenn Ford</color>, George Hamilton and Inger Stevens, but the
"J" did not stand for anything since he has no middle name. It was added to avoid confusion with a silent film actor
named Harrison Ford, who appeared in more than 80 films between 1915 and 1932 and died in 1957. Ford later said
that he was unaware of the existence of the earlier actor until he came upon a star with his own name on the <color=#3366CC>Hollywood</color>
<color=#3366CC>Walk of Fame</color>. Ford soon dropped the "J" and worked for <color=#3366CC>Universal Studios</color>, playing minor roles in many television
series throughout the late 1960s and early 1970s, including <color=#3366CC>Gunsmoke</color>, Ironside, The Virginian, The F.B.I., Love,
American Style and Kung Fu. He appeared in the western Journey to Shiloh (1968) and had an uncredited,
non-speaking role in <color=#3366CC>Michelangelo Antonioni</color>'s 1970 film Zabriskie Point as an arrested student protester. In 1968, he
also worked as a camera operator for one of <color=#3366CC>the Doors</color>' tours. French filmmaker <color=#3366CC>Jacques Demy</color> chose Ford for the lead
role of his first American film, Model Shop (1969), but the head of Columbia Pictures thought Ford had "no future" in the
film business and told Demy to hire a more experienced actor. The part eventually went to Gary Lockwood. Ford later
commented that the experience had been nevertheless a positive one because Demy was the first to show such faith in
him.
Not happy with the roles offered to him, Ford became a self-taught professional carpenter to support his then-wife and
two young sons. Clients at this time included the writers <color=#3366CC>Joan Didion</color> and John Gregory Dunne, who lived on the beach
at Malibu. Ford appears in the documentary Joan Didion: The Center Will Not Hold. He and his wife became friends of
the writers. Casting director and fledgling producer Fred Roos championed the young Ford and secured him an
audition with <color=#3366CC>George Lucas</color> for the role of Bob Falfa, which Ford went on to play in American Graffiti (1973). Ford's
relationship with Lucas profoundly affected his career later. After director <color=#3366CC>Francis Ford Coppola</color>'s film <color=#3366CC>The Godfather</color>
(1972) was a success, he hired Ford to expand his office and gave him small roles in his next two films, The
Conversation (1974) and <color=#3366CC>Apocalypse Now</color> (1979); in the latter film, Ford played an army colonel named "G. Lucas".
1977–1997: Worldwide stardom and acclaim
Ford's work in American Graffiti eventually landed him his first starring film role, when Lucas hired him to read lines for
actors auditioning for roles in Lucas's upcoming epic space-opera film <color=#3366CC>Star Wars</color> (1977). Lucas was eventually won
over by Ford's performance during these line reads and cast him as Han Solo. Star Wars became one of the most
successful and groundbreaking films of all time and brought Ford and his co-stars <color=#3366CC>Mark Hamill</color> and <color=#3366CC>Carrie Fisher</color>
widespread recognition. Ford began to be cast in bigger roles in films throughout the late 1970s, including Heroes
(1977), Force 10 from Navarone (1978) and Hanover Street (1979). He also co-starred alongside <color=#3366CC>Gene Wilder</color> in the
buddy-comedy western The Frisco Kid (1979), playing a bank robber with a heart of gold. Ford returned to star in the
successful Star Wars sequels <color=#3366CC>The Empire Strikes Back</color> (1980) and Return of the Jedi (1983), as well as the Star Wars
Holiday Special (1978). Ford wanted Lucas to kill off Han Solo at the end of Return of the Jedi, saying, "That would
have given the whole film a bottom," but Lucas refused.
Ford's status as a leading actor was solidified with <color=#3366CC>Raiders of the Lost Ark</color> (1981), an action-adventure collaboration
between Lucas and <color=#3366CC>Steven Spielberg</color> that gave Ford his second franchise role as the heroic, globe-trotting
archaeologist <color=#3366CC>Indiana Jones</color>. Like Star Wars, the film was massively successful; it became the highest-grossing film of
the year. Both Spielberg and Lucas were hesitant in casting Ford in the beginning according to Howard Kazanjian in his
book A Producer's Life. Lucas's reasons were due to having already worked with him on both American Graffiti and
Star Wars. Lucas relented after <color=#3366CC>Tom Selleck</color> was unable to accept, and Spielberg relented for that reason and after
considering his performance in The Empire Strikes Back. Ford went on to reprise the role throughout the rest of the
decade in the prequel Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom (1984) and the sequel Indiana Jones and the Last
Crusade (1989). During the June 1983 filming of Temple of Doom in London, Ford herniated a disc in his back. The
40-year-old actor was forced to fly back to Los Angeles for surgery and returned six weeks later.
Following his leading-man success as Indiana Jones, Ford played Rick Deckard in <color=#3366CC>Ridley Scott</color>'s dystopian
science-fiction film <color=#3366CC>Blade Runner</color> (1982). Compared to his experiences on the Star Wars and Indiana Jones films, Ford
had a difficult time with the production. He recalled to <color=#3366CC>Vanity Fair</color>, "It was a long slog. I didn't really find it that physically
difficult—I thought it was mentally difficult." Ford and Scott also had differing views on the nature of his character,
Deckard, that persist decades later. While not initially a success, Blade Runner became a cult classic and one of Ford's
most highly regarded films. Ford proved his versatility throughout the 1980s with dramatic parts in films such as
Witness (1985), The Mosquito Coast (1986) and Frantic (1988), as well as the romantic male lead opposite <color=#3366CC>Melanie</color>
<color=#3366CC>Griffith</color> and <color=#3366CC>Sigourney Weaver</color> in the comedy-drama Working Girl (1988). Witness and The Mosquito Coast allowed
Ford to explore his potential as a dramatic actor and both performances were widely acclaimed. Ford later recalled that
working with director <color=#3366CC>Peter Weir</color> on Witness and The Mosquito Coast were two of the best experiences of his career.
In late 1991, Ford was scheduled to star in an action-historical film titled Night Ride Down, where he would have
portrayed a Pullman Company executive whose daughter was kidnapped during a labor strike of the 1930s. Paramount
Pictures shelved the project, after Ford quit the film over script changes he disagreed with. In the next few years, Ford
became the second actor to portray Jack Ryan in two films of the film series based on the literary character created by
<color=#3366CC>Tom Clancy</color>: Patriot Games (1992) and Clear and Present Danger (1994), both co-starring Anne Archer and <color=#3366CC>James</color>
<color=#3366CC>Earl Jones</color>. Ford took over the role from <color=#3366CC>Alec Baldwin</color>, who had played Ryan in The Hunt for Red October (1990). This
led to long-lasting resentment from Baldwin, who said that he had wanted to reprise the role but Ford had negotiated
with Paramount behind his back. Ford played leading roles in other action-based thrillers throughout the decade, such
as The Fugitive (1993), The Devil's Own (1997) and Air Force One (1997). For his performance in The Fugitive, which
co-starred <color=#3366CC>Tommy Lee Jones</color>, Ford received some of the best reviews of his career, including from <color=#3366CC>Roger Ebert</color>, who
concluded that, "Ford is once again the great modern movie everyman. As an actor, nothing he does seems merely for
show and in the face of this melodramatic material he deliberately plays down, lays low, gets on with business instead
of trying to exploit the drama in meaningless acting flourishes."
Ford played more straight dramatic roles in Presumed Innocent (1990) and Regarding Henry (1991) and another
romantic lead role in Sabrina (1995), a remake of the classic 1954 film of the same name. Ford established working
relationships with many well-regarded directors during this time, including Weir, Alan J. Pakula, <color=#3366CC>Mike Nichols</color>, Phillip
Noyce and <color=#3366CC>Sydney Pollack</color>, collaborating twice with each of them. This was the most lucrative period of Ford's career.
From 1977 to 1997, he appeared in 14 films that reached the top 15 in the yearly domestic box-office rankings, 12 of
which reached the top ten. Six of the films he appeared in during this time were nominated for the Academy Award for
Best Picture, among other awards: Star Wars, Apocalypse Now, Raiders of the Lost Ark, Witness, Working Girl and
The Fugitive.
1998–2014: Established career
In the late 1990s, Ford started appearing in several critically derided and commercially disappointing films that failed to
match his earlier successes, including Six Days, Seven Nights (1998), Random Hearts (1999), K-19: The Widowmaker
(2002), Hollywood Homicide (2003), Firewall (2006) and Extraordinary Measures (2010). One exception was What Lies
Beneath (2000), which grossed over $155 million in the United States and $291 million worldwide. Ford served as an
executive producer on K-19: The Widowmaker and Extraordinary Measures, both of which were based on true events.
In 2004, Ford declined a chance to star in the thriller Syriana, later commenting that "I didn't feel strongly enough about
the truth of the material and I think I made a mistake." The role went to <color=#3366CC>George Clooney</color>, who won an Oscar and a
Golden Globe for his work. Before that, Ford had passed on a role in another Stephen Gaghan-written film, that of
Robert Wakefield in Traffic, which went to <color=#3366CC>Michael Douglas</color>.
In 2008, Ford enjoyed success with the release of Indiana Jones and the Kingdom of the Crystal Skull, the first Indiana
Jones film in 19 years and another collaboration with Lucas and Spielberg. The film received generally positive reviews
and was the second-highest-grossing film worldwide in 2008. Ford later said he would like to star in another sequel "if it
didn't take another 20 years to digest." Other 2008 work included Crossing Over, directed by Wayne Kramer. In the
film, Ford plays an ICE/Homeland Security Investigations Special Agent, working alongside Ashley Judd and Ray
Liotta. He also narrated a feature documentary film about the <color=#3366CC>Dalai Lama</color>, Dalai Lama Renaissance.
Ford filmed the medical drama Extraordinary Measures in 2009 in <color=#3366CC>Portland, Oregon</color>. Released on January 22, 2010,
the film also starred Brendan Fraser and Alan Ruck. Also in 2010, he co-starred in the film Morning Glory, along with
<color=#3366CC>Rachel McAdams</color>, <color=#3366CC>Diane Keaton</color> and Patrick Wilson. Although the film was a disappointment at the box office, Ford's
performance was well received by critics, some of whom thought it was his best role in years. In July 2011, Ford starred
alongside <color=#3366CC>Daniel Craig</color> and Olivia Wilde in the science-fiction/western hybrid film Cowboys & Aliens. To promote the
film, he appeared at <color=#3366CC>San Diego Comic-Con</color> and, apparently surprised by the warm welcome, told the audience, "I just
wanted to make a living as an actor. I didn't know about this." Also in 2011, Ford starred in Japanese commercials
advertising the video game Uncharted 3: Drake's Deception for the <color=#3366CC>PlayStation 3</color>.
2013 began a trend that saw Ford accepting more diverse supporting roles. That year, he co-starred in the corporate
espionage thriller Paranoia with Liam Hemsworth and <color=#3366CC>Gary Oldman</color>, whom he had previously worked with in Air Force
One, and also appeared in Ender's Game, 42 and Anchorman 2: The Legend Continues.
Ford's performance as <color=#3366CC>Branch Rickey</color> in the film 42 was praised by many critics and garnered Ford a nomination as
best supporting actor for the Satellite Awards. Initially, Brian Helgeland was hesitant to cast Ford, seeking a character
actor for the role of Rickey. However, Ford's persistence and dedication to the role, including studying Rickey's life and
adopting significant physical transformations, won Helgeland over. Ford's commitment to embodying Rickey involved
wearing a fat suit, prosthetics and mastering Rickey's distinctive voice and mannerisms. He researched Rickey's life,
listened to recordings from the Baseball Hall of Fame and worked with a voice coach to capture Rickey's distinct
speech. "I loved the language of the guy, I loved his style," Ford noted. In a 2023 interview with James Hibberd of The
Hollywood Reporter, Ford said Branch Rickey is one of his roles he is most proud of.
In 2014, he appeared in The Expendables 3 and the following year, co-starred with Blake Lively in the romantic drama
The Age of Adaline to positive reviews.
2015–present: Return to franchise roles and Shrinking
Ford reprised the role of Han Solo in the long-awaited Star Wars sequel Star Wars: The Force Awakens (2015), which
was highly successful, like its predecessors. During filming on June 11, 2014, Ford suffered what was said to be a
fractured ankle when a hydraulic door fell on him. He was airlifted to John Radcliffe Hospital in <color=#3366CC>Oxford</color>, England, for
treatment. Ford's son Ben Ford released details on his father's injury, saying that his ankle would likely need a plate
and screws and that filming could be altered slightly, with the crew needing to shoot Ford from the waist up for a short
time until he recovered. Ford made his return to filming in mid-August, after a two-month layoff as he recovered from
his injury. Ford's character was killed off in The Force Awakens, but it was subsequently announced, via a casting call,
that Ford would return in some capacity as Solo in Episode VIII. In February 2016, when the cast for Episode VIII was
confirmed, it was indicated that Ford would not reprise his role in the film after all. When Ford was asked whether Solo
could come back in "some form", he replied, "Anything is possible in space." He eventually made an uncredited
appearance as a vision in Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker (2019).
On February 26, 2015, Alcon Entertainment announced Ford would reprise his role as Rick Deckard in Denis
Villeneuve's science fiction sequel film Blade Runner 2049. The film and Ford's performance, was very well received by
critics upon its release in October 2017. Scott Collura of IGN called it a "deep, rich, smart film that's visually awesome
and full of great sci-fi concepts" and Ford's role "a quiet, sort of gut-wrenching interpretation to Deckard and what he
must've gone through in the past three decades." The film grossed $259.3 million worldwide, short of the estimated
$400 million that it needed to break even. In 2019, Ford had his first voice role in an animated film, as a dog named
Rooster in The Secret Life of Pets 2. With filming of a fifth Indiana Jones film delayed by a year, Ford headlined a
big-budget adaptation of <color=#3366CC>Jack London</color>'s <color=#3366CC>The Call of the Wild</color>, playing prospector John Thornton. The film was released
in February 2020 to a mixed critical reception and its theatrical release was shortened due to the impact of the
COVID-19 pandemic on the film industry.
In 2022, Ford was cast to star alongside <color=#3366CC>Helen Mirren</color> in the Paramount+ western drama series 1923. The two had
previously starred together 36 years earlier in The Mosquito Coast. The series premiered in December 2022 to positive
reviews and it is set to run for a total of two seasons. That same year, it was announced that Ford would star in the
Apple TV+ comedy drama series Shrinking. The series premiered in January 2023 to positive reviews, with Ford
receiving praise for his performance. In a 2023 interview with <color=#3366CC>The Hollywood Reporter</color>, it was revealed that he
accepted the roles in both 1923 and Shrinking despite there not being a script at the time. For his work in Shrinking,
Ford was nominated for several awards including a <color=#3366CC>Golden Globe</color> for Best Supporting Actor, a Critics' Choice
Television Award for Best Supporting Actor in a Comedy Series, his first Screen Actors Guild Award for Outstanding
Performance by a Male Actor in a Comedy Series and his first <color=#3366CC>Emmy Award</color> for Outstanding Supporting Actor in a
Comedy Series.
Ford reprised the role of Indiana Jones in Indiana Jones and the Dial of Destiny (2023), which he later stated would be
his last appearance as the character. The film received generally positive reviews, with many critics highlighting Ford's
performance. In February 2025, Ford starred alongside Anthony Mackie (the new <color=#3366CC>Captain America</color>) as Thaddeus Ross
in the <color=#3366CC>Marvel Cinematic Universe</color> film Captain America: Brave New World, replacing <color=#3366CC>William Hurt</color> after the latter's
death. That same month, he brought attention to an ongoing strike by video game actors when he voiced support for
Troy Baker playing the role of Indiana Jones in the video game Indiana Jones and the Great Circle, speaking out
against the use of <color=#3366CC>artificial intelligence</color>.
Personal life
Ford has been married three times and has four biological children and one adopted child. He was first married to Mary
Marquardt from 1964 until their divorce in 1979. They had two sons, born in 1966 and 1969. The older son once
co-owned Ford's Filling Station, a gastropub located at Terminal 5 in <color=#3366CC>Los Angeles International Airport</color>. The younger
son is owner of the Ludwig Clothing company and previously owned Strong Sports Gym and the Kim Sing Theater.
Ford's second marriage was to screenwriter Melissa Mathison from March 1983 until their separation in 2000; they
divorced in 2004. They had a son, born in 1987 and a daughter, born in 1990. Mathison died in 2015.
Ford began dating actress Calista Flockhart after they met at the 2002 Golden Globe Awards. He proposed to
Flockhart over Valentine's Day weekend in 2009. They married on June 15, 2010, in <color=#3366CC>Santa Fe, New Mexico</color>, where
Ford was filming Cowboys & Aliens. They are the parents of a son, born in 2001, whom Flockhart had adopted before
meeting Ford. Ford and Flockhart live on an 800 acre ranch in Jackson, Wyoming, where he has lived since the 1980s
and approximately half of which he has donated as a nature reserve. They retain a house in the Brentwood
neighborhood of Los Angeles. Ford is one of Hollywood's most private actors, guarding much of his personal life.
Although Ford's fans have speculated that he has <color=#3366CC>social anxiety disorder</color>, he said in 2023 that he instead has "an
abhorrence of boring situations".
In her 2016 autobiography The Princess Diarist, <color=#3366CC>Carrie Fisher</color> wrote that she and Ford had a three-month affair in 1976
during the filming of <color=#3366CC>Star Wars</color>.
Aviation
Ford is a licensed pilot of both <color=#3366CC>fixed-wing aircraft</color> and helicopters. On several occasions, he has provided emergency
helicopter services at the request of local authorities in <color=#3366CC>Wyoming</color>. In 2000, he airlifted an <color=#3366CC>EMT</color> to a 20-year-old hiker
who was suffering from dehydration on Table Mountain. The following year, he was flagged down in his helicopter by a
13-year-old Boy Scout who got lost near <color=#3366CC>Yellowstone National Park</color>.
Ford began flight training in the 1960s at Wild Rose Idlewild Airport in Wild Rose, Wisconsin, flying in a Piper PA-22
Tri-Pacer, but at $15 an hour, he could not afford to continue the training. In the mid-1990s, he bought a used
Gulfstream II and asked one of his pilots, Terry Bender, to give him flying lessons. They started flying a Cessna 182
Skylane out of Jackson, Wyoming, later switching to Teterboro Airport in Teterboro, New Jersey, flying a Cessna 206 in
which he made his first solo flight.
Ford's aircraft are kept at Santa Monica Airport. His Bell 407 helicopter is often hangered at Jackson and has been
used by Ford in two mountain rescues during his assigned duty time with Teton County Search and Rescue. During
one of the rescues, Ford recovered a lost and disoriented hiker. She boarded his helicopter and promptly vomited into
one of the rescuers' caps, unaware of who the pilot was until much later; "I can't believe I barfed in Harrison Ford's
helicopter!" she said later.
Ford flies his de Havilland Canada DHC-2 Beaver (registration N28S) more than any of his other aircraft and has
repeatedly said that he likes this aircraft and the sound of its Pratt & Whitney R-985 radial engine. According to Ford, it
had been flown in the CIA's Air America operations and was riddled with bullet holes that had to be patched up.
In March 2004, Ford became chairman of the Experimental Aircraft Association (EAA)'s Young Eagles program,
founded by then-EAA president Tom Poberezny and fellow actor-pilot Cliff Robertson. Ford was asked to take the
position by Greg Anderson, Senior Vice President of the EAA at the time, to replace General <color=#3366CC>Chuck Yeager</color>, who was
vacating the post that he had held for many years. Ford at first was hesitant, but later accepted the offer and has made
appearances with the Young Eagles at the EAA AirVenture Oshkosh gathering at Oshkosh, Wisconsin, for two years.
In July 2005, at the gathering in Oshkosh, Ford agreed to accept the position for another two years. He has flown over
280 children as part of the Young Eagles program, usually in his DHC-2 Beaver, which can seat the actor and five
children. Ford stepped down as program chairman in 2009 and was replaced by Captain Chesley Sullenberger and
First Officer Jeff Skiles. He is involved with the EAA chapter in Driggs, Idaho, just over the <color=#3366CC>Teton Range</color> from Jackson,
Wyoming. On July 28, 2016, Ford flew the two millionth Young Eagle at the EAA AirVenture convention, making it the
most successful youth aviation introduction program in history.
As of 2009, Ford appears in Internet advertisements for General Aviation Serves America, a campaign by the advocacy
group Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association (AOPA). He has also appeared in several independent aviation
documentaries, including Wings Over the Rockies (2009), Flying the Feathered Edge: The Bob Hoover Project (2014)
and Living in the Age of Airplanes (2015).
Ford is an honorary board member of the humanitarian aviation organization Wings of Hope, and has made several
trips to Washington, D.C., to fight for pilots' rights. He has also donated substantial funds to <color=#3366CC>aerobatic</color> champion Sean
Tucker's charitable program, The Bob Hoover Academy (named after legendary aviator Bob Hoover), which educates
at-risk teens in central California and teaches them how to fly.
Incidents
On August 22, 1987, Ford was traveling as a passenger with <color=#3366CC>Clint Eastwood</color> and Sondra Locke aboard a Gulfstream III
when the jet developed an engine fire and stuck landing gear during a Paris-to-L.A. flight and was forced to land in
Bangor, Maine. The charter company owning the G-3 sent another jet and mechanics to Bangor and the group flew out
on that plane the next day.
On October 23, 1999, Ford was involved in the crash of a Bell 206L4 LongRanger helicopter. The NTSB accident
report states that Ford was piloting the aircraft over the Lake Piru riverbed near Santa Clarita, California, on a routine
training flight. While making his second attempt at an autorotation with powered recovery, the aircraft was unable to
recover power after the sudden drop in altitude. It landed hard and skidded forward in the loose gravel before flipping
onto its side. Neither Ford nor the instructor pilot suffered any injuries, though the helicopter was seriously damaged.
On March 5, 2015, Ford's plane, believed to be a Ryan PT-22 Recruit, made an emergency landing on the Penmar Golf
Course in Venice, California, after it lost engine power. He was taken to Ronald Reagan UCLA Medical Center, where
he was reported to be in fair to moderate condition. Ford suffered a broken <color=#3366CC>pelvis</color> and broken ankle during the accident,
as well as other injuries.
On February 13, 2017, Ford landed an Aviat Husky at John Wayne Airport in Orange County, California, on the taxiway
left of runway 20L. A <color=#3366CC>Boeing 737</color> was holding short of the runway on the taxiway when Ford overflew them.
On April 24, 2020, at the Los Angeles Hawthorne Airport while piloting his Husky, Ford crossed a runway where
another aircraft was landing. According to the FAA, the two planes were about 3,600 feet from each other and there
was no danger of collision. A representative of Ford later said that he "misheard" an instruction given to him by air
traffic control.
Activism
Environmental work
Ford is vice-chair of Conservation International, an American nonprofit environmental organization headquartered in
Arlington, Virginia. The organization's intent is to protect <color=#3366CC>nature</color>. Since 1992, Ford has lent his voice to a series of public
service messages promoting environmental involvement for EarthShare, an American federation of environmental and
conservation charities. He has acted as a spokesperson for Restore Hetch Hetchy, a non-profit organization dedicated
to restoring <color=#3366CC>Yosemite National Park</color>'s Hetch Hetchy Valley to its original condition. Ford also appears in the
documentary series Years of Living Dangerously, which reports on people affected by and seeking solutions to climate
change.
In 1993, the arachnologist Norman Platnick named a new species of spider Calponia harrisonfordi and in 2002 the
<color=#3366CC>entomologist</color> <color=#3366CC>Edward O. Wilson</color> named a new <color=#3366CC>ant</color> species Pheidole harrisonfordi (in recognition of Harrison's work as
Vice Chairman of Conservation International). The Peruvian snake species Tachymenoides harrisonfordi was named
for Ford in 2023.
In September 2013, Ford, while filming an environmental documentary in <color=#3366CC>Indonesia</color>, interviewed the Indonesian
<color=#3366CC>Forestry</color> Minister, Zulkifli Hasan. After the interview, Ford and his crew were accused of "harassing state institutions"
and publicly threatened with <color=#3366CC>deportation</color>. Questions within the interview concerned the Tesso Nilo National Park,
<color=#3366CC>Sumatra</color>. It was alleged the Minister of Forestry was given no prior warning of questions nor the chance to explain the
challenges of catching illegal loggers. Ford was provided an audience with the Indonesian President, <color=#3366CC>Susilo Bambang</color>
<color=#3366CC>Yudhoyono</color>, during which he expressed concerns regarding Indonesia's environmental degradation and the
government efforts to <color=#3366CC>address climate change</color>. In response, the President explained Indonesia's commitment to
preserving its oceans and forests.
In 2019, on behalf of Conservation International, Ford gave an impassioned speech during the United Nations' Climate
Action Summit in New York on the <color=#3366CC>destruction of the Amazon rainforest</color> and its effect on climate change for the rest of
the world. Ford urged his audience to listen to 'angry young people' trying to make a difference in the situation,
emphasizing, "The most important thing we can do for them is to get the hell out of their way."
In 2025, the E.O. Wilson Biodiversity Foundation gave Ford its inaugural E.O. Wilson Legacy Award for Transformative
Conservation Leadership.
Political views
Like his parents, Ford is a lifelong <color=#3366CC>Democrat</color>. On September 7, 1995, Ford testified before the U.S. Senate Foreign
Relations Committee in support of the <color=#3366CC>Dalai Lama</color> and an independent <color=#3366CC>Tibet</color>. In 2007, he narrated the documentary
Dalai Lama Renaissance. In 2000, Ford donated $1,000 to the presidential campaigns of Bill Bradley, <color=#3366CC>Al Gore</color> and
<color=#3366CC>John McCain</color>. In 2003, he publicly condemned the <color=#3366CC>Iraq War</color> and called for "regime change" in the United States. He
also criticized <color=#3366CC>Hollywood</color> for making movies which were "more akin to video games than stories about human life and
relationships" and he called for more gun control in the United States.
<color=#3366CC>Roman Polanski</color> won an Oscar for directing The Pianist in 2003, but avoids setting foot on US soil after he plead guilty
to unlawful sexual intercourse with a minor and then fled the country. Ford brought the Oscar statuette to Paris and
presented it to Polanski. In 2009, Ford signed a petition calling for the release of Polanski, who had been arrested in
Switzerland in relation to his 1977 charge for drugging and raping a 13-year-old girl.
After <color=#3366CC>Republican</color> presidential candidate <color=#3366CC>Donald Trump</color> said his favorite role of Ford's was Air Force One because he
"stood up for America", Ford responded that it was just a film and made critical statements against Trump's presidential
bid. Ford endorsed <color=#3366CC>Joe Biden</color>'s 2020 presidential campaign against Trump. He said that he wanted to "encourage
people to support candidates that will support the environment" and felt that under Trump, the U.S. had "lost some of
our credibility in the world". Along with <color=#3366CC>Mark Hamill</color>, Ford worked with the anti-Trump Republican group The Lincoln
Project to produce and narrate a 2020 election ad attacking Trump's disparaging of <color=#3366CC>Anthony Fauci</color>. On November 2,
2024, he endorsed <color=#3366CC>Kamala Harris</color>'s 2024 presidential campaign.
Archaeology
Following on his success portraying the archaeologist <color=#3366CC>Indiana Jones</color>, Ford also plays a part in supporting the work of
professional <color=#3366CC>archaeologists</color>. He serves as a General Trustee on the Governing Board of the Archaeological Institute of
America (AIA), North America's oldest and largest organization devoted to the world of archaeology. Ford assists them
in their mission of increasing public awareness of archaeology and preventing looting and the illegal antiquities trade.
Acting credits and accolades
Throughout his career, Ford has received significant recognition for his work in the entertainment industry. In 1986, he
was nominated for Best Actor at the 58th Academy Awards for his performance in Witness, a role for which he also
received BAFTA and Golden Globe nominations in the same category. Three additional Golden Globe nominations
went to Ford in 1987, 1994 and 1996 for his performances in The Mosquito Coast, The Fugitive and Sabrina. In 2000,
he was the recipient of the AFI Life Achievement Award from the American Film Institute for his body of work,
presented to him by two of his closest collaborators and fellow industry giants, George Lucas and Steven Spielberg. In
2002, he was given the Cecil B. DeMille Award, another career achievement honor, from the Hollywood Foreign Press
Association at the 59th Golden Globe Awards ceremony. On May 30, 2003, Ford received a star on the <color=#3366CC>Hollywood</color>
<color=#3366CC>Walk of Fame</color>.
In 2006, he received the Jules Verne Award, given to an actor who has "encouraged the spirit of adventure and
imagination" throughout their career. He was presented with the first-ever Hero Award at the 2007 Scream Awards for
his many iconic roles, including Indiana Jones and Han Solo (both of which earned him a collective three Saturn
Awards for Best Actor in 1982, 2024 and 2016, respectively) and in 2008 he received the Spike TV's Guy's Choice
Award for "Brass Balls". In 2015, Ford received the Albert R. Broccoli Britannia Award for Worldwide Contribution to
Entertainment from BAFTA Los Angeles. In 2018, Ford was honored by the SAG-AFTRA Foundation with the Artists
Inspiration Award for both his acting and philanthropic work alongside fellow honoree <color=#3366CC>Lady Gaga</color>. SAG-AFTRA
Foundation Board President JoBeth Williams in the press release said, "Harrison Ford is an acting legend in every
known galaxy, but what many do not know are the decades of philanthropic service and leadership he has given to
Conservation International to help protect our planet."
Other prestigious film honors for Ford include an Honorary Cesar, an Honorary Palme d'Or from the <color=#3366CC>Cannes Film</color>
<color=#3366CC>Festival</color>, the Career Achievement Award from the Hollywood Film Awards, the Kirk Douglas Award for Excellence in
Film from the Santa Barbara International Film Festival, the Box Office Star of the Century Award from the National
Association of Theatre Owners and the Lifetime Achievement Award from both the Locarno Film Festival and the

Ford has also been honored multiple times for his involvement in <color=#3366CC>general aviation</color>, receiving the Living Legends of
Aviation Award and the Experimental Aircraft Association's Freedom of Flight Award in 2009, the Wright Brothers
Memorial Trophy in 2010, and the Al Ueltschi Humanitarian Award in 2013. Flying magazine ranked him number 48 on

In March 2026, Ford received the SAG-AFTRA Life Achievement Award for his career achievements and humanitarian
accomplishments. In his acceptance speech, Ford said he was not an "overnight success", moving between acting and

<color=#3366CC>Star Wars</color>.
Earth

Earth is the third <color=#3366CC>planet</color> from the <color=#3366CC>Sun</color> and the only <color=#3366CC>astronomical object</color> known to <color=#3366CC>harbor life</color>. This is made possible by
Earth being an ocean world, the only one in the <color=#3366CC>Solar System</color> sustaining liquid surface water. Almost all of Earth's
water is contained in its <color=#3366CC>ocean</color>, which covers 70.8% of <color=#3366CC>Earth's crust</color>. The remaining 29.2% of Earth's crust is <color=#3366CC>land</color>,
which is predominantly located within Earth's <color=#3366CC>land hemisphere</color> in the form of <color=#3366CC>continental</color> landmasses. Most of Earth's
land is at least somewhat <color=#3366CC>humid</color> and covered by vegetation, while large <color=#3366CC>ice sheets</color> at Earth's polar deserts retain more
water than Earth's <color=#3366CC>groundwater</color>, lakes, rivers, and <color=#3366CC>atmospheric water</color> combined. Earth's crust consists of slowly moving
<color=#3366CC>tectonic plates</color>, which interact to produce mountain ranges, <color=#3366CC>volcanoes</color>, and earthquakes. Earth has <color=#3366CC>a liquid outer core</color>
that generates a <color=#3366CC>magnetosphere</color> capable of deflecting most of the destructive <color=#3366CC>solar winds</color> and <color=#3366CC>cosmic radiation</color>.
Earth has <color=#3366CC>a dynamic atmosphere</color>, which sustains Earth's surface conditions and protects it from most <color=#3366CC>meteoroids</color> and

<color=#3366CC>ultraviolet light at entry</color>. It is composed primarily of <color=#3366CC>nitrogen</color> and <color=#3366CC>oxygen</color>. <color=#3366CC>Water vapor</color> is widely present in the
atmosphere, <color=#3366CC>forming clouds</color> that cover most of the planet. The water vapor acts as a <color=#3366CC>greenhouse gas</color> and, together
with other greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, particularly <color=#3366CC>carbon dioxide</color> (CO2), creates the conditions for both
liquid surface water and water vapor to persist via the capturing of <color=#3366CC>energy from the Sun's light</color>. This process maintains
the current average surface temperature of 14.76 C, at which water is liquid under normal <color=#3366CC>atmospheric pressure</color>.
Differences in the amount of captured energy between geographic regions (as with the <color=#3366CC>equatorial region</color> receiving more
sunlight than the polar regions) drive <color=#3366CC>atmospheric</color> and <color=#3366CC>ocean currents</color>, producing a global <color=#3366CC>climate system</color> with different
climate regions, and a range of weather phenomena such as <color=#3366CC>precipitation</color>, allowing components such as <color=#3366CC>carbon</color> and
<color=#3366CC>nitrogen</color> to <color=#3366CC>cycle</color>.
Earth is <color=#3366CC>rounded</color> into <color=#3366CC>an ellipsoid</color> with a circumference of about 40000 km. It is the densest planet in the Solar System.
Of the four <color=#3366CC>rocky planets</color>, it is the largest and most massive. Overall, Earth is the sixth largest object in the Solar
System after the Sun and the <color=#3366CC>outer planets</color>. Earth is about eight light-minutes (1 <color=#3366CC>AU</color>) away from the Sun and <color=#3366CC>orbits it</color>,
taking a year (about 365.25 days) to complete one revolution. <color=#3366CC>Earth rotates</color> around its own axis in slightly less than a
day (in about 23 hours and 56 minutes). <color=#3366CC>Earth's axis of rotation</color> is tilted with respect to the perpendicular to its orbital
plane around the Sun, producing seasons. Earth is <color=#3366CC>orbited</color> by one permanent <color=#3366CC>natural satellite</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Moon</color>, which orbits
Earth at 384400 km—1.28 light seconds—and is roughly a quarter as wide as Earth. The Moon's gravity helps stabilize
Earth's <color=#3366CC>axis</color>, causes <color=#3366CC>tides</color>, and <color=#3366CC>gradually slows Earth's rotation</color>. Likewise, Earth's gravitational pull has already made
the Moon's rotation <color=#3366CC>tidally locked</color>, keeping the same <color=#3366CC>near side</color> facing Earth.
Earth, like most other bodies in the Solar System, <color=#3366CC>formed about 4.5 billion years ago</color> from gas and dust in the <color=#3366CC>early</color>
<color=#3366CC>Solar System</color>. The formation of the ocean and the subsequent <color=#3366CC>development of life</color> occurred during the first billion years
of <color=#3366CC>Earth's history</color>. Life spread globally and has been altering Earth's atmosphere and surface, leading to the <color=#3366CC>Great</color>
<color=#3366CC>Oxidation Event</color> two billion years ago. <color=#3366CC>Humans</color> emerged 300,000 years ago in Africa and have spread across every
continent on Earth. Humans depend on Earth's <color=#3366CC>biosphere</color> and natural resources for their survival, but have <color=#3366CC>increasingly</color>
<color=#3366CC>impacted the planet's environment</color>. Humanity's current impact on Earth's climate and biosphere is unsustainable,
threatening the livelihood of humans and many other forms of life, and <color=#3366CC>causing widespread extinctions</color>.
Etymology
The <color=#3366CC>Modern English</color> word Earth developed, via <color=#3366CC>Middle English</color>, from an <color=#3366CC>Old English</color> noun most often spelled eorðe. It
has cognates in every <color=#3366CC>Germanic language</color>, from which erþō has been reconstructed. In its earliest attestation, the word
eorðe was used to translate the many senses of Latin terra and Greek: the ground, its soil, dry land, the human world,
the surface of the world (including the sea), and the globe itself. As with <color=#3366CC>Roman</color> Terra (or Tellus) and Greek <color=#3366CC>Gaia</color>, Earth
may have been a personified goddess in <color=#3366CC>Germanic paganism</color>: late <color=#3366CC>Norse mythology</color> included Jörð ('Earth'), a giantess
often given as the mother of <color=#3366CC>Thor</color>.
Historically, Earth has been written in lowercase. During the <color=#3366CC>Early Middle English</color> period, its <color=#3366CC>definite sense</color> as "the
globe" began being expressed using the phrase the earth. By the period of <color=#3366CC>Early Modern English</color>, capitalization of
nouns began to prevail, and the earth was also written the Earth, particularly when referenced along with other
heavenly bodies. More recently, the name is sometimes simply given as Earth, by analogy with the names of the <color=#3366CC>other</color>
<color=#3366CC>planets</color>, though earth and forms with the earth remain common. <color=#3366CC>House styles</color> now vary: Oxford spelling recognizes the
lowercase form as the more common, with the capitalized form an acceptable variant. Another convention capitalizes
Earth when appearing as a name, such as a description of the "Earth's atmosphere", but employs the lowercase when
it is preceded by the, such as "the atmosphere of the earth". It almost always appears in lowercase in colloquial
expressions such as "what on earth are you doing?"
The name Terra is occasionally used in scientific writing; it also sees use in science fiction to distinguish humanity's
inhabited planet from others, while in poetry Tellus has been used to denote personification of the Earth. Terra is also
the name of the planet in some <color=#3366CC>Romance languages</color>, languages that evolved from Latin, like Italian and Portuguese,
while in other Romance languages the word gave rise to names with slightly altered spellings, like the Spanish Tierra
and the French Terre. The Latinate form Gaea of the Greek poetic name <color=#3366CC>Gaia</color> ( or ) is rare, though the alternative
spelling Gaia has become common due to the <color=#3366CC>Gaia hypothesis</color>, in which case its pronunciation is rather than the more
traditional English.
There are a number of adjectives for the planet Earth. The word earthly is derived from Earth. From the Latin Terra
comes terran, terrestrial, and (via French) terrene, and from the Latin Tellus comes tellurian and telluric.
Natural history
Formation
The oldest material found in the <color=#3366CC>Solar System</color> is dated to 4.5682 <color=#3366CC>Ga</color> (billion years) ago. By 4.54 Ga, the primordial
Earth had formed. The bodies in <color=#3366CC>the Solar System formed and evolved</color> with the Sun. In theory, a <color=#3366CC>solar nebula</color> partitions
a volume out of a <color=#3366CC>molecular cloud</color> by gravitational collapse, which begins to spin and flatten into a <color=#3366CC>circumstellar disk</color>,
and then the planets grow out of that disk with the Sun. A nebula contains gas, ice grains, and <color=#3366CC>dust</color> (including

<color=#3366CC>primordial nuclides</color>). According to <color=#3366CC>nebular theory</color>, <color=#3366CC>planetesimals</color> formed by <color=#3366CC>accretion</color>, with the primordial Earth being
estimated as likely taking anywhere from 70 to 100 million years to form.
Estimates of the age of the Moon range from 4.5 Ga to significantly younger. The <color=#3366CC>leading hypothesis</color> is that it was
formed by accretion from material loosed from Earth after a <color=#3366CC>Mars</color>-sized object with about 10% of Earth's mass, named
<color=#3366CC>Theia</color>, collided with Earth. It hit Earth with a glancing blow, and some of its mass merged with Earth. Between
approximately 4.0 and 3.8 Ga, numerous <color=#3366CC>asteroid impacts</color> during the <color=#3366CC>Late Heavy Bombardment</color> caused significant
changes to the greater surface environment of the Moon and, by inference, to that of Earth.
After formation
<color=#3366CC>Earth's atmosphere</color> and oceans were formed by <color=#3366CC>volcanic activity</color> and outgassing. Water vapor from these sources
condensed into the oceans, augmented by water and ice from asteroids, <color=#3366CC>protoplanets</color>, and <color=#3366CC>comets</color>. Sufficient water to
fill the oceans may have been on Earth since it formed. In this model, atmospheric <color=#3366CC>greenhouse gases</color> kept the oceans
from freezing when the newly forming Sun had only 70% of its <color=#3366CC>current luminosity</color>. By 3.5 Ga, <color=#3366CC>Earth's magnetic field</color> was
established, which helped prevent the atmosphere from being stripped away by the <color=#3366CC>solar wind</color>.
As the molten outer layer of Earth cooled, it <color=#3366CC>formed</color> the first solid <color=#3366CC>crust</color>, which is thought to have been mafic in
composition. The first <color=#3366CC>continental crust</color>, which was more felsic in composition, formed by the <color=#3366CC>partial melting</color> of this mafic
crust. Hadean-aged zircon grains found in <color=#3366CC>Western Australia</color>, dating back as far as 4.4 Ga, provide the oldest direct
evidence of Earth's surface, indicating that felsic continental crust and liquid water existed within 140–160 million years
of the planet's formation. There are two main models of how this initial small volume of continental crust evolved to
reach its current abundance: (1) a relatively steady growth up to the present day, which is supported by the radiometric
dating of continental crust globally and (2) an initial rapid growth in the volume of continental crust during the <color=#3366CC>Archean</color>,
forming the bulk of the continental crust that now exists, which is supported by isotopic evidence from <color=#3366CC>hafnium</color> in
<color=#3366CC>zircons</color> and <color=#3366CC>neodymium</color> in sedimentary rocks. The two models and the data that support them can be reconciled by
large-scale recycling of the continental crust, particularly during the early stages of Earth's history.
New continental crust forms as a result of <color=#3366CC>plate tectonics</color>, a process ultimately driven by the continuous loss of heat
from Earth's interior. Over <color=#3366CC>the period</color> of hundreds of millions of years, tectonic forces have caused areas of continental
crust to group together to form <color=#3366CC>supercontinents</color> that have subsequently broken apart. At approximately 750 <color=#3366CC>Ma</color>, one of
the earliest known supercontinents, <color=#3366CC>Rodinia</color>, began to break apart. The continents later recombined to form <color=#3366CC>Pannotia</color> at
600 Ma, then finally <color=#3366CC>Pangaea</color>, which also began to break apart at 180 Ma.
The most recent pattern of <color=#3366CC>ice ages</color> began about 40 Ma, and then intensified during the <color=#3366CC>Pleistocene</color> about 3 Ma. <color=#3366CC>High-</color>
and middle-latitude regions have since undergone repeated cycles of glaciation and thaw, repeating about every
21,000, 41,000, and 100,000 years. The <color=#3366CC>Last Glacial Period</color>, colloquially called the "last ice age", covered large parts of
the continents, to the middle latitudes, in ice and ended about 11,700 years ago.
Origin of life and evolution
<color=#3366CC>Chemical reactions</color> led to the first self-replicating molecules about four billion years ago. A half billion years later, the
<color=#3366CC>last common ancestor of all current life</color> arose. The evolution of <color=#3366CC>photosynthesis</color> allowed the Sun's energy to be
harvested directly by life forms. The resultant <color=#3366CC>molecular oxygen</color> (O2) accumulated in the atmosphere and, due to
interaction with ultraviolet solar radiation, formed a protective <color=#3366CC>ozone layer</color> (O3) in the upper atmosphere. The
incorporation of smaller cells within larger ones resulted in the <color=#3366CC>development of complex cells</color> called <color=#3366CC>eukaryotes</color>. True
multicellular organisms formed as cells within <color=#3366CC>colonies</color> became increasingly specialized. Aided by the absorption of
harmful <color=#3366CC>ultraviolet radiation</color> by the ozone layer, life colonized Earth's surface. Among the earliest <color=#3366CC>fossil</color> evidence for life
are microbial mat fossils found in 3.48 billion-year-old <color=#3366CC>sandstone</color> in <color=#3366CC>Western Australia</color>, biogenic <color=#3366CC>graphite</color> found in 3.7
billion-year-old metasedimentary rocks in Western Greenland, and remains of biotic material found in 4.1
billion-year-old rocks in Western Australia. The <color=#3366CC>earliest direct evidence of life</color> on Earth is contained in 3.45
billion-year-old <color=#3366CC>Australian</color> rocks showing fossils of <color=#3366CC>microorganisms</color>.
During the <color=#3366CC>Neoproterozoic</color>, 1000 Ma, much of Earth might have been covered in ice. This hypothesis has been termed
"<color=#3366CC>Snowball Earth</color>", and it is of particular interest because it preceded the <color=#3366CC>Cambrian explosion</color>, when multicellular life
forms significantly increased in complexity. Following the Cambrian explosion, 535 Ma, there have been at least five
major <color=#3366CC>mass extinctions</color> and many minor ones. Apart from the proposed current <color=#3366CC>Holocene extinction</color> event, the <color=#3366CC>most</color>
<color=#3366CC>recent</color> was 66 Ma, when <color=#3366CC>an asteroid impact</color> triggered the extinction of non-avian dinosaurs and other large reptiles, but
largely spared small animals, such as insects, <color=#3366CC>mammals</color>, lizards, and birds. Mammalian life has diversified over the
past 66 million years, and several million years ago, an African <color=#3366CC>ape</color> species gained the ability to stand upright. This
facilitated tool use and encouraged communication that provided the nutrition and stimulation needed for a larger brain,
which led to the <color=#3366CC>evolution of humans</color>. The <color=#3366CC>development of agriculture</color>, and then <color=#3366CC>civilization</color>, led to humans having an
<color=#3366CC>influence on Earth</color> and the nature and quantity of other life forms that continues to this day.
Future
Earth's expected long-term future is tied to that of the Sun. Over the next 1.1 billion years, solar luminosity will increase
by 10%, and over the next 3.5 billion years by 40%. Earth's increasing surface temperature will accelerate the inorganic
carbon cycle, possibly reducing CO2 concentration to levels lethally low for current plants (10 ppm for <color=#3366CC>C4</color>
<color=#3366CC>photosynthesis</color>) in approximately 100 million years. A lack of vegetation would result in the loss of oxygen in the
atmosphere, making current animal life impossible. Due to the increased luminosity, Earth's mean temperature may
reach 100 C in 1.5 billion years, and all ocean water will evaporate and be lost to space, which may trigger a runaway
greenhouse effect, within an estimated 1.6 to 3 billion years. Even if the Sun were stable and eternal, a significant
fraction of the water in the modern oceans would descend into the <color=#3366CC>mantle</color>, due to reduced steam venting from
mid-ocean ridges as the core of the Earth slowly cools.
The Sun will <color=#3366CC>evolve</color> to become a <color=#3366CC>red giant</color> in about 5 billion years. Models predict that the Sun will expand to roughly 1
AU, about 250 times its present radius. Earth's fate is less clear. As a red giant, the Sun will lose roughly 30% of its
mass, so, without tidal effects, Earth will move to an orbit 1.7 AU from the Sun when the star reaches its maximum
radius, otherwise, with tidal effects, it may enter the Sun's atmosphere and be vaporized, with the heavier elements
sinking to the core of the dying sun. A new study published in 2026 has suggested that the Earth is likely to survive the
Sun's <color=#3366CC>asymptotic giant branch</color> phase.
Composition and structure
Earth is a <color=#3366CC>rocky planet</color> and an ocean world, the only one in the <color=#3366CC>Solar System</color> with liquid surface water. Among all rocky
Solar System objects, it is the most massive, 81 times that of Earth's <color=#3366CC>Moon</color>; and among all planetary-mass objects of
the Solar System, it is the object with the highest density.
Earth has a rounded shape, through <color=#3366CC>hydrostatic equilibrium</color>, with an equatorial diameter of 12756 km, making it the
fifth-largest planetary-sized and largest terrestrial object of the Solar System, and 3.7 times larger than Earth's Moon.
Chemical composition

<color=#3366CC>Earth's mass</color> is approximately 5.97×10^24 kg. It is composed mostly of iron (32.1% <color=#3366CC>by mass</color>), <color=#3366CC>oxygen</color> (30.1%), <color=#3366CC>silicon</color>

(15.1%), <color=#3366CC>magnesium</color> (13.9%), <color=#3366CC>sulfur</color> (2.9%), <color=#3366CC>nickel</color> (1.8%), <color=#3366CC>calcium</color> (1.5%), and <color=#3366CC>aluminum</color> (1.4%), with the remaining
1.2% consisting of trace amounts of other elements. Due to <color=#3366CC>gravitational separation</color>, the core is primarily composed of
the denser elements: iron (88.8%), with smaller amounts of nickel (5.8%), sulfur (4.5%), and less than 1% trace
elements. The most common rock constituents of the crust are <color=#3366CC>oxides</color>. Over 99% of the <color=#3366CC>crust</color> is composed of various
oxides of eleven elements, principally oxides containing silicon (the <color=#3366CC>silicate minerals</color>), aluminum, iron, calcium,
magnesium, potassium, or sodium.
Internal structure
Earth's interior, like that of the other terrestrial planets, is divided into layers by their <color=#3366CC>chemical</color> or physical (<color=#3366CC>rheological</color>)
properties. The outer layer is a chemically distinct <color=#3366CC>silicate</color> solid crust, which is underlain by a highly <color=#3366CC>viscous</color> solid
mantle. The crust is separated from the mantle by the <color=#3366CC>Mohorovičić discontinuity</color>. The thickness of the crust varies from
about 6 km under the oceans to 30 – 50 km for the continents. The crust and the cold, rigid top of the <color=#3366CC>upper mantle</color> are
collectively known as the lithosphere, which is divided into independently moving tectonic plates.
Beneath the lithosphere is the <color=#3366CC>asthenosphere</color>, a relatively low-viscosity layer on which the lithosphere rides. Important
changes in crystal structure within the mantle occur at 410 and 660 km below the surface, spanning a <color=#3366CC>transition zone</color>
that separates the upper and lower mantle. Beneath the mantle, an extremely low-viscosity liquid <color=#3366CC>outer core</color> lies above
a solid <color=#3366CC>inner core</color>. Earth's inner core may be rotating at a slightly higher <color=#3366CC>angular velocity</color> than the remainder of the
planet, advancing by 0.1–0.5° per year, although both somewhat higher and much lower rates have also been
proposed. The radius of the inner core is about one-fifth of that of Earth. The density increases with depth.
Internal heat
The major contributors to Earth's internal heat are primordial heat (heat left over from Earth's formation) and radiogenic
heat (heat produced by radioactive decay). The major heat-producing <color=#3366CC>isotopes</color> within Earth are <color=#3366CC>potassium-40</color>,
<color=#3366CC>uranium-238</color>, and thorium-232. At the center, the temperature may be up to 6000 C, and the pressure could reach 360
GPa. Because much of the heat is provided by radioactive decay, scientists postulate that early in Earth's history,
before isotopes with short half-lives were depleted, Earth's heat production was much higher. At approximately 3 Gyr,
twice the present-day heat would have been produced, increasing the rates of <color=#3366CC>mantle convection</color> and plate tectonics,
and allowing the production of uncommon <color=#3366CC>igneous rocks</color> such as <color=#3366CC>komatiites</color> that are rarely formed today.
The mean heat loss from Earth is 87 mW/m2, for a global heat loss of 4.42×10^13 W. A portion of the core's thermal
energy is transported toward the crust by <color=#3366CC>mantle plumes</color>, a form of convection consisting of upwellings of
higher-temperature rock. These plumes can produce <color=#3366CC>hotspots</color> and <color=#3366CC>flood basalts</color>. More of the heat in Earth is lost
through plate tectonics, by mantle upwelling associated with <color=#3366CC>mid-ocean ridges</color>. The final major mode of heat loss is
through conduction through the lithosphere, the majority of which occurs under the oceans.
Tectonic plates
Earth's mechanically rigid outer layer of <color=#3366CC>Earth's crust</color> and <color=#3366CC>upper mantle</color>, the <color=#3366CC>lithosphere</color>, is divided into tectonic plates.
These plates are rigid segments that move relative to each other at one of three boundary types: at <color=#3366CC>convergent</color>
<color=#3366CC>boundaries</color>, two plates come together; at <color=#3366CC>divergent boundaries</color>, two plates are pulled apart; and at <color=#3366CC>transform</color>
<color=#3366CC>boundaries</color>, two plates slide past one another laterally. Along these plate boundaries, earthquakes, <color=#3366CC>volcanic activity</color>,
<color=#3366CC>mountain-building</color>, and <color=#3366CC>oceanic trench</color> formation can occur. The tectonic plates ride on top of the <color=#3366CC>asthenosphere</color>, the
solid but less-viscous part of the upper mantle that can flow and move along with the plates.
As the tectonic plates migrate, oceanic crust is <color=#3366CC>subducted</color> under the leading edges of the plates at convergent
boundaries. At the same time, the upwelling of mantle material at divergent boundaries creates mid-ocean ridges. The
combination of these processes recycles the oceanic crust back into the mantle. Due to this recycling, most of the
ocean floor is less than 100 Myr old. The oldest oceanic crust is located in the Western Pacific and is estimated to be
200 Myr old. By comparison, the oldest dated continental crust is 4030 Myr, although zircons have been found
preserved as clasts within Eoarchean sedimentary rocks that give ages up to 4400 Myr, indicating that at least some
continental crust existed at that time.

The seven major plates are the <color=#3366CC>Pacific</color>, <color=#3366CC>North American</color>, <color=#3366CC>Eurasian</color>, <color=#3366CC>African</color>, <color=#3366CC>Antarctic</color>, <color=#3366CC>Indo-Australian</color>, and <color=#3366CC>South</color>

<color=#3366CC>American</color>. Other notable plates include the <color=#3366CC>Arabian Plate</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Caribbean Plate</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Nazca Plate</color> off the west coast of
South America, and the <color=#3366CC>Scotia Plate</color> in the southern Atlantic Ocean. The Australian Plate fused with the Indian Plate
between 50 Ma. The fastest-moving plates are the oceanic plates, with the <color=#3366CC>Cocos Plate</color> advancing at a rate of 75
mm/year and the Pacific Plate moving 52 – 69 mm/year. At the other extreme, the slowest-moving plate is the South
American Plate, progressing at a typical rate of 10.6 mm/year.
Crust
Earth's crust may be divided into <color=#3366CC>oceanic</color> and <color=#3366CC>continental</color> crust. The oceanic crust is predominantly <color=#3366CC>basaltic</color>, while the
continental crust has more lower-density materials such as <color=#3366CC>granite</color>, metamorphic rocks, and sediments, which—while
covering nearly 75% of the continental surfaces—make only about 5% of the mass of the crust.
While the oceanic crust is covered by the <color=#3366CC>ocean</color>, the ocean also covers continental crust, the <color=#3366CC>continental shelves</color>,
which makes these parts of the ocean <color=#3366CC>shelf seas</color>. The oceanic crust forms large <color=#3366CC>oceanic basins</color> with features like

<color=#3366CC>abyssal plains</color>, <color=#3366CC>seamounts</color>, <color=#3366CC>submarine volcanoes</color>, <color=#3366CC>oceanic trenches</color>, submarine canyons, oceanic plateaus, and a
globe-spanning <color=#3366CC>mid-ocean ridge</color> system. The terrain of the ocean floor has an average depth of roughly 3.8 km.
Surface
Earth's surface is the boundary between the atmosphere and the solid Earth and oceans. The surface is continually

being shaped by internal <color=#3366CC>plate tectonic</color> processes including <color=#3366CC>earthquakes</color> and <color=#3366CC>volcanism</color>; by <color=#3366CC>weathering</color> and <color=#3366CC>erosion</color>
driven by ice, water, wind and temperature; and by biological processes including the growth and decomposition of
biomass into <color=#3366CC>soil</color>.
Earth's surface has an area of about 510 e6km2 and can be divided into two <color=#3366CC>hemispheres</color>: by <color=#3366CC>latitude</color> into the polar

<color=#3366CC>Northern</color> and <color=#3366CC>Southern</color> hemispheres, by <color=#3366CC>longitude</color> into the continental <color=#3366CC>Eastern</color> and <color=#3366CC>Western</color> hemispheres, or roughly as
<color=#3366CC>Water</color> and <color=#3366CC>Land hemispheres</color>.
Most of Earth's surface is ocean water: 70.8% or 361 e6km2. This vast pool of salty water is often called the world
ocean, and makes Earth with its dynamic <color=#3366CC>hydrosphere</color> a water world or ocean world. Indeed, in Earth's early history,
the ocean may have covered Earth completely. The world ocean is commonly divided into the Pacific Ocean, Atlantic
Ocean, Indian Ocean, Southern Ocean, and Arctic Ocean, from largest to smallest. At Earth's <color=#3366CC>polar regions</color>, the <color=#3366CC>ocean</color>

<color=#3366CC>surface</color> is covered by seasonally variable amounts of <color=#3366CC>sea ice</color> that often connects with polar land, <color=#3366CC>permafrost</color>, and <color=#3366CC>ice</color>
<color=#3366CC>sheets</color>, forming polar ice caps.
Earth's land covers 29.2%, or 149 e6km2 of Earth's surface. The land surface includes many <color=#3366CC>islands</color> around the globe,
but most of the land surface is taken up by the four continental landmasses, which are (in descending order):
<color=#3366CC>Africa-Eurasia</color>, <color=#3366CC>America</color>, <color=#3366CC>Antarctica</color>, and Australia. These landmasses are further broken down and grouped into the
<color=#3366CC>continents</color>. Land can be covered by surface water, snow, ice, artificial structures, or vegetation. Most of Earth's land
hosts vegetation, but considerable amounts of land are <color=#3366CC>ice sheets</color> (10%, not including the equally large area of land
under <color=#3366CC>permafrost</color>) or <color=#3366CC>deserts</color> (33%).
The <color=#3366CC>pedosphere</color> is the outermost layer of Earth's land surface and is composed of <color=#3366CC>soil</color> and subject to <color=#3366CC>soil formation</color>
processes. Soil is crucial for land to be arable. Earth's total <color=#3366CC>arable land</color> is 10.7% of the land surface, with 1.3% being
permanent cropland. Earth has an estimated 16.7 e6km2 of cropland and 33.5 e6km2 of pastureland.
Surface topography
Earth's surface <color=#3366CC>topography</color> comprises both the <color=#3366CC>topography of the ocean surface</color> and the <color=#3366CC>shape</color> of Earth's land surface.

The <color=#3366CC>terrain</color> of the land surface varies greatly and consists of mountains, <color=#3366CC>deserts</color>, <color=#3366CC>plains</color>, <color=#3366CC>plateaus</color>, and other <color=#3366CC>landforms</color>.
The elevation of the land surface varies from a low point of -418 m at the <color=#3366CC>Dead Sea</color>, to a maximum altitude of 8848 m
at the top of <color=#3366CC>Mount Everest</color>. The mean height of land above sea level is about 797 m.
Shape
Due to Earth's rotation, <color=#3366CC>its shape</color> is that of an <color=#3366CC>ellipsoid</color>, <color=#3366CC>bulging at its equator</color>; its diameter is 43 km longer there than at
its poles. Earth's shape also has local <color=#3366CC>topographic</color> variations; the largest local variations, like the <color=#3366CC>Mariana Trench</color>
(10925 m below local sea level), shorten Earth's average radius by 0.17%, and <color=#3366CC>Mount Everest</color> (8848 m above local sea
level) lengthens it by 0.14%. Since Earth's surface is farthest out from its <color=#3366CC>center of mass</color> at its equatorial bulge, the
summit of the volcano <color=#3366CC>Chimborazo</color> in Ecuador (6384.4 km) is its farthest point out. Parallel to the rigid land topography,
<color=#3366CC>the ocean exhibits a more dynamic topography</color>.
To measure the local variation of Earth's topography, <color=#3366CC>geodesy</color> employs an idealized Earth producing a <color=#3366CC>geoid</color> shape.
Such a shape is obtained if the ocean is idealized, covering Earth completely and without any perturbations such as
tides and winds. The result is a smooth but irregular geoid surface, providing a mean sea level as a reference level for
topographic measurements.
Gravity and magnetic field
Magnetic field
The main part of Earth's magnetic field is generated in the core, the site of a dynamo process that converts the kinetic
energy of thermally and compositionally driven convection into electrical and magnetic field energy. The field extends
outwards from the core, through the mantle, and up to Earth's surface, where it is approximately a <color=#3366CC>dipole</color>. The poles of
the dipole are located close to Earth's geographic poles. At the equator of the magnetic field, the magnetic-field
strength at the surface is 3.05 <color=#3366CC>T</color>, with a <color=#3366CC>magnetic dipole moment</color> of 7.79 Am2 at epoch 2000, decreasing nearly 6% per
century (although it remains stronger than its long-term average). The convection movements in the core are chaotic;
the magnetic poles drift and periodically change alignment. This causes secular variation of the main field and <color=#3366CC>field</color>
<color=#3366CC>reversals</color> at irregular intervals averaging a few times every million years. The most recent reversal occurred
approximately 700,000 years ago.
The extent of Earth's magnetic field in space defines the <color=#3366CC>magnetosphere</color>. Ions and electrons of the solar wind are
deflected by the magnetosphere; solar wind pressure compresses the day-side of the magnetosphere to about 10
Earth radii, and extends the night-side magnetosphere into a long tail. Because the velocity of the solar wind is greater
than the speed at which waves propagate through the solar wind, a supersonic bow shock precedes the day-side
magnetosphere within the solar wind. Charged particles are contained within the magnetosphere; the plasmasphere is
defined by low-energy particles that essentially follow magnetic field lines as Earth rotates. The ring current is defined
by medium-energy <color=#3366CC>particles</color> that drift relative to the geomagnetic field, but with paths that are still dominated by the
magnetic field, and the <color=#3366CC>Van Allen radiation belts</color> are formed by high-energy particles whose motion is essentially
random, but contained in the magnetosphere. During <color=#3366CC>magnetic storms</color> and substorms, charged particles can be
deflected from the outer magnetosphere and especially the magnetotail, directed along field lines into Earth's
<color=#3366CC>ionosphere</color>, where atmospheric atoms can be excited and ionized, causing an <color=#3366CC>aurora</color>.
Gravitational field
The gravity of Earth is the <color=#3366CC>acceleration</color> that is imparted to objects due to the distribution of mass within Earth. Near
Earth's surface, <color=#3366CC>gravitational acceleration</color> is approximately 9.8 m/s2. Local differences in topography, geology, and
deeper tectonic structure cause local and broad regional differences in Earth's gravitational field, known as gravity
anomalies. The Hill sphere, or the sphere of gravitational influence, of Earth is about 1.5 e6km in radius. This is the
maximum distance at which Earth's gravitational influence is stronger than that of the more distant Sun and planets.
Objects must orbit Earth within this radius, or they can become unbound by the gravitational perturbation of the Sun.
Moon and orbital space
Moon
The Moon is a relatively large, <color=#3366CC>terrestrial</color>, planet-like natural satellite, with a diameter about one-quarter of Earth's. It is
the largest moon in the Solar System relative to the size of its planet, although <color=#3366CC>Charon</color> is larger relative to the dwarf
planet <color=#3366CC>Pluto</color>. The natural satellites of other planets are also referred to as "moons", after Earth's. The Moon and Earth
orbit a common <color=#3366CC>barycenter</color> every 27.32 days relative to the background stars. When combined with the Earth–Moon
system's common orbit around the Sun, the period of the synodic month, from new moon to new moon, is 29.53 days.
Viewed from the <color=#3366CC>celestial north pole</color>, the motion of Earth, the Moon, and their axial rotations are all counterclockwise.
Viewed from Earth, the Moon is just far enough away to have almost the same apparent-sized disk as the Sun. The
<color=#3366CC>angular sizes</color> (or <color=#3366CC>solid angles</color>) of these two bodies match because, although the Sun's diameter is about 400 times as
large as the Moon's, it is also 400 times more distant. This allows total and annular solar eclipses to occur on Earth.
The orbital planes are not precisely aligned: the Earth-Moon plane is tilted up to ±5.1 degrees against the Earth–Sun
plane (the <color=#3366CC>ecliptic</color>). Without this tilt, there would be an eclipse every two weeks, alternating between <color=#3366CC>lunar eclipses</color> and
<color=#3366CC>solar eclipses</color>.
The gravitational attraction between Earth and the Moon causes <color=#3366CC>lunar tides</color> on Earth. The same effect on the Moon has
led to its <color=#3366CC>tidal locking</color>: its rotation period is the same as the time it takes to orbit Earth. As a result, it always presents
the same face to the planet. As the Moon orbits Earth, different parts of its face are illuminated by the Sun, leading to
the <color=#3366CC>lunar phases</color>. Due to their <color=#3366CC>tidal interaction</color>, the Moon recedes from Earth at the rate of approximately 38 mm/yr.
Over millions of years, these tiny modifications—and the lengthening of Earth's day by about 23 s/yr—add up to
significant changes. During the <color=#3366CC>Ediacaran</color> period (approximately 620 Ma), for example, there were 400±7 days in a
year, with each day lasting 21.9±0.4 hours.
The Moon may have dramatically affected the development of life by moderating the planet's climate. <color=#3366CC>Paleontological</color>
evidence and computer simulations show that Earth's axial tilt is stabilized by tidal interactions with the Moon. Some
theorists think that without this stabilization against the <color=#3366CC>torques</color> applied by the Sun and planets to Earth's equatorial
bulge, the rotational axis might be chaotically unstable, exhibiting large changes over millions of years, as is the case
for Mars, though this is disputed.
The most widely accepted theory of the Moon's origin, the <color=#3366CC>giant-impact hypothesis</color>, states that it formed from the
collision of a Mars-size protoplanet called Theia with the early Earth. This hypothesis explains the Moon's relative lack
of iron and volatile elements and the fact that its composition is nearly identical to that of Earth's crust. Computer
simulations suggest that two blob-like remnants of this protoplanet could be inside the Earth.
Asteroids and artificial satellites
Earth's <color=#3366CC>co-orbital asteroid</color> population consists of quasi-satellites, objects with a <color=#3366CC>horseshoe orbit</color>, and <color=#3366CC>trojans</color>. There are
at least seven quasi-satellites, including 469219 Kamooalewa, ranging in diameter from 10 m to 5000 m. A trojan
asteroid companion, is <color=#3366CC>librating</color> around the leading <color=#3366CC>Lagrange triangular point</color>, L4, in <color=#3366CC>Earth's orbit</color> around the Sun. The
tiny <color=#3366CC>near-Earth asteroid</color> makes close approaches to the Earth–Moon system roughly every twenty years. During these
approaches, it can orbit Earth for brief periods of time.
As of 2023 5, there are 7,560 operational, human-made <color=#3366CC>satellites</color> orbiting Earth. There are also inoperative satellites,
including Vanguard 1, the oldest satellite currently in orbit, and over 16,000 pieces of tracked space debris. Earth's
largest artificial satellite is the <color=#3366CC>International Space Station</color> (ISS).
Orbit and rotation
Rotation
Earth's rotation period relative to the Sun—its mean solar day—is 86,400 seconds of mean solar time (86,400.0025 <color=#3366CC>SI</color>
seconds). Because Earth's solar day is now slightly longer than it was during the 19th century due to <color=#3366CC>tidal deceleration</color>,
each day varies between 0 and 2 ms longer than the mean solar day.
Earth's rotation period relative to the fixed stars, called its stellar day by the International Earth Rotation and Reference
Systems Service (IERS), is 86,164.0989 seconds of mean solar time (UT1), or 23h 56m 4.0989s. Earth's rotation
period relative to the <color=#3366CC>precessing</color> or moving mean <color=#3366CC>March equinox</color> (when the Sun is at 90° on the equator) is
86,164.0905 seconds of mean solar time (UT1) (23h 56m 4.0905s). Thus the sidereal day is shorter than the stellar day
by about 8.4 ms.
